section.title: The Remnant of Israel
section.sectionRationale: Having shown that Israel stumbled over the stone of Christ and was largely disobedient, Paul now asks the burning question: has God then rejected His people? His answer is an emphatic no. Paul himself is living proof, an Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin. As in Elijah's dark day, when the prophet thought he stood alone, God had kept seven thousand for Himself, so now at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace. And if it is by grace, it cannot be by works, or grace would cease to be grace. The rest were hardened, given eyes that do not see.
section.thesis: God has not rejected the people He foreknew; He has always preserved a remnant chosen by grace, and grace by its very nature excludes works, so that salvation stands on God's free choice and not on human achievement, while the rest are hardened in their unbelief.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the question answered, God has not rejected His people, and Paul is the proof; the pattern of the remnant, as in Elijah's day so now, a remnant chosen by grace and not by works; and the hardening of the rest, eyes that do not see.

units.label: Has God rejected His people?
units.note: certainly not, Paul himself is the proof

verses.text: I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not! I am an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin.
God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says about Elijah, how he appealed to God against Israel:
“Lord, they have killed Your prophets and torn down Your altars. I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well”?

units.label: A remnant chosen by grace
units.note: as in Elijah's day, and if by grace then not by works

verses.text: And what was the divine reply to him? “I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”
In the same way, at the present time there is a {{leimma|remnant}} chosen by {{charis|grace}}.
And if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace.

units.label: The rest were hardened
units.note: eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear

verses.text: What then? What Israel was seeking, it failed to obtain, but the {{ekloge|elect}} did. The others were {{poroo|hardened}},
as it is written: “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that could not see, and ears that could not hear, to this very day.”
And David says: “May their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution to them.
May their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and their backs be bent forever.”

leimma.gloss: A remnant, what is left over, those who remain. Drawn from the prophets, where a faithful remnant of Israel always survived judgment, the word names the small company God keeps for Himself. It is not the impressive majority but the preserved few, and their existence proves God has not cast off His people but is quietly keeping His promise.

charis.gloss: Grace, unmerited favor, God's free gift. The remnant is chosen by grace, not gathered by human merit. Grace is the sovereign kindness of God that gives what could never be earned; it is the ground on which the remnant stands and the very opposite of works.

ekloge.gloss: Election, choice, selection. Paul says the elect obtained what Israel as a whole sought in vain. The word points to God's gracious choosing, His decision to set His love on a people, so that those who obtain righteousness do so because God first chose them, not because they first chose Him.

poroo.gloss: To harden, to make callous, to render dull or insensible. The others were hardened, their hearts made unresponsive so that eyes do not see and ears do not hear. This hardening is a real and sobering judgment, yet Paul will show it is neither total nor final, for God's purpose of mercy runs beneath even this.

basic.context: Paul has just described Israel largely refusing the gospel and stumbling over Christ. Now he asks whether this means God has abandoned His ancient people altogether. His answer is a firm no. He points to himself, a true Israelite, and then to the days of Elijah, when the prophet felt utterly alone but God had kept seven thousand faithful. So it is now: God has preserved a remnant, and He has done so by grace, not by anything they achieved.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as the opening of Paul's answer to a fear his argument might raise: if Israel has largely fallen away, has God's word failed? Paul appeals to the Old Testament pattern, Elijah on Mount Horeb, to show that a faithful remnant is exactly how God has always worked. Verse 6 is the hinge: grace and works are mutually exclusive as grounds of standing before God. Verses 8 to 10 gather Scripture to describe the hardening of the rest.
basic.originalLanguages: The key words are leimma, the remnant God keeps for Himself; charis, the grace by which they are chosen; ekloge, God's electing choice, so that the elect obtain what the nation as a whole missed; and poroo, the hardening that came upon the others, dulling their eyes and ears.
basic.typology: Elijah's seven thousand who never bowed to Baal foreshadow the remnant of grace in every age. The faithful few preserved through judgment point to the church, kept not by their strength but by God's choice, and ultimately to Christ, the true and faithful Israelite in whom the remnant is gathered.
basic.christ: Paul the Israelite is himself a trophy of grace, saved by the risen Christ who met him on the Damascus road. The remnant is chosen in Christ and by the grace that comes through Him. What Israel sought, a right standing with God, is found only in Christ, obtained by the elect through faith in Him and never by works.
basic.god: God is faithful; He has not rejected the people He foreknew. He is sovereign in grace, reserving a remnant for Himself just as He reserved seven thousand in Elijah's day. He is also just; the hardening of the rest is His righteous judgment on persistent unbelief. Grace and judgment both display His freedom.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 19 records Elijah's despair and God's reply about the seven thousand. Isaiah 10 promises that a remnant will return. Romans 9 has already introduced God's electing purpose. Ephesians 2 declares salvation by grace, not works, so no one may boast.
basic.oneStory: Through the whole Old Testament, judgment never wiped out God's people entirely; a remnant always survived by grace. Here Paul shows that same pattern continuing in his own day and in himself. The story of God keeping a people for Himself runs straight on into the church, and it stands on grace from first to last.

context.literary:
Romans 11 opens with the same device Paul has used all through the letter: a question that sounds like the argument's possible end, answered by 'Certainly not!' The Greek is me genoito, 'may it never be,' and it appears at Romans 3:4, 6:2 and 9:14 each time at a moment when a reader might draw a conclusion that would slander God. Here the slander would be that God has thrown away His people.

The passage has three panels. Verses 1 and 2a are the thesis and the first proof, Paul himself. Verses 2b to 6 are the second proof, an Old Testament story from Elijah's life, which Paul applies in verse 5 with the little phrase 'in the same way' and then reflects on in verse 6. Verses 7 to 10 are a sober coda about the rest, with two quotations that sound like judgment.

The hinge is verse 6. It looks like a parenthesis, but the whole passage turns on it, because the word 'remnant' could have been heard as a reward for the few who stayed faithful. Paul closes that reading at once: if it is by grace it is not by works. Then verse 7 resumes the question 'What then?' that Paul has asked so often, and gives an answer in three clauses that are almost a miniature of chapters 9 to 11: Israel as a whole sought and failed, the elect obtained, the others were hardened.

Look also at the shape of the quotations. Verse 3 and 4 quote Elijah and God's reply. Verse 8 quotes a composite of Deuteronomy and Isaiah. Verses 9 and 10 quote David. So the Law, the Prophets and the Writings are all summoned, as in chapter 10, to speak for the two halves of the story, mercy and hardening. The passage ends on a note of heaviness that chapter 11 does not leave unanswered, for verse 11 will pick up at once with another question: did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery?
context.historical:
Elijah's story belongs to the ninth century before Christ, in the reign of Ahab and Jezebel, when the northern kingdom was drenched in Baal worship and the prophets of the LORD were hunted. In 1 Kings 18 Elijah faces the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, and in chapter 19 he runs for his life to Horeb, the mountain of the covenant, and says in despair that he is the only one left, 1 Kings 19:10 and 19:14. God's answer includes the work He still has for Elijah and then the quiet fact that He has reserved seven thousand in Israel, 1 Kings 19:18. The number is probably a round number of completeness, but the point is the same either way: the nation seemed to be gone, and God had kept more than the prophet knew.

Paul's own world had a similar shape. The majority of Jews in the Diaspora did not accept the gospel, and many in Judea actively opposed it. Yet from the first day there had been thousands of Jewish believers, Acts 2:41 and Acts 21:20, the Jerusalem church was Jewish, and the earliest missionaries were Jewish. Paul is writing to Rome knowing that his collection for the saints in Jerusalem is about to be delivered, Romans 15:25-27, so the church of Jewish believers is not an abstraction to him.

He mentions that he is of the tribe of Benjamin, as he does in Philippians 3:5. The tribe had a particular place in Israel's memory: it was the tribe of King Saul, Paul's own Hebrew name was Saul, and Benjamin stayed with Judah when the kingdom split, 1 Kings 12:21. The little detail adds to Paul's credentials as a loyal member of the covenant people, not a defector.

The quotations in verses 9 and 10 come from a psalm of David, Psalm 69, a prayer of a righteous sufferer surrounded by enemies. The table in it is probably the table of feasting and fellowship. Some readers think Paul's setting is the festivals and sacrifices where people felt secure, which turned into a trap. Such an inversion was well known in the prophets, who warned that religious ritual without obedience becomes a snare, Isaiah 1:11-15 and Amos 5:21-24.
context.canonical:
The remnant is one of the great threads of the Old Testament, and Paul draws on its main strands. It first appears in the flood and in the story of Lot, and then in the prophets, who use it as both warning and promise. Isaiah named a son Shear-jashub, 'a remnant will return,' Isaiah 7:3 and 10:21-22, so that the child himself was a sermon. The same prophet wrote that without survivors left by the LORD of Hosts Israel would have been like Sodom, Isaiah 1:9, and Paul had already quoted both Isaiah texts in Romans 9:27-29. Micah speaks of the 'remnant of His inheritance' whom God pardons, Micah 7:18, and Zephaniah promises a humble and lowly people who will take refuge in the name of the LORD, Zephaniah 3:12-13.

Paul also relies on a counter thread, the failure of Israel to see. Deuteronomy 29:4 had said that to this day the LORD had not given a mind to understand, eyes to see or ears to hear, though they had seen the signs in Egypt. Isaiah 29:10 spoke of a spirit of deep sleep. Isaiah 6:9-10 is the great text on eyes that cannot see, and the Gospels quote it of the crowds who heard Jesus' parables, Matthew 13:14-15, and of those who did not believe, John 12:40. Paul's composite of verse 8 therefore fits into a river of earlier texts.

The Psalms quotation in verses 9 and 10 comes from Psalm 69, which the New Testament applies to Jesus several times: the zeal for God's house, John 2:17; the hatred without cause, John 15:25; the insults that fell on the sufferer, Romans 15:3; and the gall and vinegar, Matthew 27:34 and 27:48. Paul uses it here as David's words against those who persist in rejecting the righteous sufferer.

Finally, the remnant theme finds its New Testament landing in the line of believers: Paul's own testimony, the Jerusalem church and the later promise that all Israel will be saved, Romans 11:26. Revelation 7:4-8 numbers the tribes who are sealed, and Revelation 12:17 speaks of those who keep the commandments of God and hold the testimony of Jesus. The remnant never disappears from the Bible's last pages.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul is answering a fear, and it is a fear for God's reputation before it is a fear for Israel's future. If God promised Israel everything and Israel is now largely outside the gospel, then either the promises failed or God is unreliable. Paul's reply is that God's word has not failed, 9:6, and the proof is a visible fact, not a theory: there are Jewish believers, Paul among them.

He also means to protect the Gentile believers from a conclusion they might draw. If the nation is hardened, perhaps the church can think of itself as having replaced Israel. Paul begins closing that door here and will shut it firmly in verse 18. The remnant means the story is still Israel's story and the church has entered it.

And he means to preserve grace as the only footing. The idea of a faithful remnant could be heard as 'the best of Israel survived.' Paul says, with the last emphasis of the paragraph, that survival is a gift. This is for the sake of the remnant, so that they do not boast, and for the sake of the rest, so that they do not think the door is closed because of their record. Nobody enters or fails to enter by merit. The whole of salvation is by an electing and gracious God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verse 5 is a description of a present fact, 'at the present time there is a remnant.' It does not tell readers to measure their congregation by its numbers or to take comfort in small size as such. The story of Elijah should not be turned into a rule that faithful people are always few; Acts also records thousands coming to faith in a day.

What Paul does prescribe is a way of reading hard times. When faithful people feel isolated, like Elijah, they should not conclude that the cause is lost. God's knowledge of His own is wider than their sight, and Elijah's sense of being alone was mistaken, as seven thousand showed. That is pastoral comfort, and Paul has placed it right in the middle of a hard argument.

The hardening passages in verses 8 to 10 are description, and they are a reflection on a particular people at a particular time. They are not an instruction to treat any group as beyond hope, nor a licence to pronounce on anyone's final state. Paul's own history is the best evidence: he was once among those whose eyes could not see, and the risen Christ opened them, Acts 9:17-18.

debates.question: What does 'foreknew' mean in verse 2, and who are 'His people'?

views.label: God set His love on them beforehand
views.case: The verb is the same one Paul used in Romans 8:29, and in the Old Testament knowing is often a word of covenant love, as in Amos 3:2 and Jeremiah 1:5. 'Whom He foreknew' then means the people God chose to know in love, and that is why they cannot be thrown away. This is the Reformed reading.

views.label: God foresaw their response
views.case: Others take the verb as foreknowledge of faith: God knew beforehand who would trust Him. The difficulty is that verse 2 describes the whole people, not a subset, and the verse is a defence of the nation, so a reading that depends on individual foreseen faith is a weaker fit with the clause, though it is held by many Arminian interpreters.

debates.bearing: On either reading the verse says that God's relationship to Israel was settled before Israel acted, which is the reason rejection is unthinkable. The disagreement is about the reason behind the knowing, not about whether God stays faithful.

debates.question: Who is hardened, and who does the hardening in verses 7 and 8?

views.label: God is the agent
views.case: The verb in verse 7 is a passive without a stated agent, and the quotation says 'God gave them a spirit of stupor.' This follows the pattern of Pharaoh in Romans 9:17-18 and of Isaiah 6. Hardening is a judicial act in which God confirms people in the direction they have chosen.

views.label: People harden themselves and God confirms it
views.case: Paul's vocabulary elsewhere speaks of human hardness, as in Romans 2:5, 'your stubborn and unrepentant heart,' and the Old Testament often says that a person hardened his own heart. On this view God's act and the person's act are two sides of one story, with the human act coming first.

debates.bearing: Both agree that Paul does not treat hardening as a reason to stop appealing. The verses he uses to describe it end 'to this very day,' which implies a time frame, and the next verses will show it is not final.

debates.question: Does the elect of verse 7 mean individuals chosen for salvation, or the believing group within Israel?

views.label: Individuals chosen by God
views.case: The noun 'election' in verses 5 and 7, with 'chosen by grace,' sits beside Romans 8:33 and 9:11, where the same family of words refers to God's purpose in choosing. This reading stresses that the remnant is made, not discovered.

views.label: The believing community, chosen in Christ
views.case: Some stress that the elect are the people of the remnant considered as a body, not as separate decisions, and that the point is that grace is behind the existence of the whole body. They point to Ephesians 1:4, 'chose us in Him.'

debates.bearing: The passage itself is concerned with the shape of the whole people. Whichever reading is held, the point of verses 5 and 6 stands: God's choice is the ground, and works are excluded.

study.originalLanguages:
The question of verse 1 uses the verb apotheo, to push away or repudiate, which is the word that the Greek Old Testament uses in Psalm 94:14 where the LORD will not forsake His people, and in the similar promise at 1 Samuel 12:22. Paul's wording is meant to ring with these texts. When he says God has not pushed away the people He 'foreknew,' he uses proginosko, the word of Romans 8:29, and in the Bible knowing of this kind belongs to relationship and choice.

Verse 2 introduces the Elijah story with an odd phrase, en Elia, literally 'in Elijah.' It is a way of citing a section of Scripture by its principal figure, the way we might say 'in the Elijah cycle.' The next verbs are careful too. Elijah 'appeals' or pleads, entynchano, against Israel, which is the same verb used in Romans 8:34 of Christ interceding for believers. The contrast is bitter: Elijah's intercession becomes an accusation, and Christ's is for the elect.

The remnant of verse 5 is leimma, a word taken from the verb 'to leave.' Paul had used the related hypoleimma in 9:27 when he quoted Isaiah. In verse 4 God says literally 'I have left for Myself,' using the same stem, so the remnant is what God leaves, not what is left over by chance. The addition 'for Myself' makes the point: they are His.

Verse 5 says the remnant is chosen 'by grace,' kat' eklogen charitos, 'according to an election of grace.' Eklogē is the noun for choosing out. In verse 7 it comes back with the article as a collective, 'the election,' translated 'the elect.' The same word occurs in 9:11 and again in 11:28, so it is a thread across these three chapters.

Verse 6 sets two conditions side by side, 'by grace' and 'by works,' and treats them as mutually exclusive. The sentence uses the language of exclusion, and the rule is set out as a matter of logic: grace that is partly earned would not be grace.

In verse 7, Israel 'was seeking,' epizeteo, in the imperfect tense, which means a continued searching, and 'did not obtain,' epitygchano, a one time result. Their sincere and long labour yielded nothing. The elect 'obtained,' and Paul does not say what, because the object is what Israel sought, a standing before God, 9:31 to 10:4.

The word for 'hardened' is poroo, the same verb John 12:40 uses of hearts, and in verse 25 the noun porosis appears, 'hardening in part,' as it does in Mark 3:5 where Jesus grieves at hard hearts. The 'stupor' of verse 8 is katanyxis, a deep drowsiness, from Isaiah 29:10 in the Greek Bible, while the part about eyes and ears recalls Deuteronomy 29:4. The 'snare and trap' of verse 9 are pagis and thera, language of hunters, and 'retribution' is antapodoma, a repayment. In verse 10 the backs 'bent' use the verb sygkampto, a bowed posture of someone under a load.

typology.fulfillment: Elijah thought the covenant community had shrunk to one man, and God showed him a hidden company. Paul reads this as a pattern: in every age of apparent collapse God keeps a people for Himself, and in his day that remnant is the Jewish believers. The correspondence is a hidden and preserved faithful few. The escalation is that the remnant in Paul's time are gathered around a risen Messiah and are the first fruits of a larger ingathering, Romans 11:16. The type falls short because Elijah's seven thousand were distinguished by what they refused, bowing to Baal, while the remnant of grace is defined by what God gave, not by what they refused.

Isaiah's son Shear-jashub, 'a remnant will return,' was a walking sign that judgment would not be the end, Isaiah 7:3 and 10:20-22. The remnant came back from exile and rebuilt, Ezra 2. Paul takes the same sign and sees it in the believing Jews of his generation, who were saved through the gospel and so carried the promise forward. The escalation is that return from Babylon becomes a return to God Himself through Christ, and the remnant becomes the root from which others are grafted in, 11:17. The type falls short because the earlier remnant restored a city, and the later remnant belongs to a kingdom not of this world, John 18:36.

typology.type: Paul the Benjaminite as a living sign
typology.fulfillment: Paul offers himself as exhibit A, a man who was among the persecutors and who is now the apostle. In 1 Timothy 1:15-16 he calls himself the worst of sinners and an example of Christ's patience to those who would believe. His life shows the shape of Israel's own story, a zealous people who opposed the Lord and are then seized by mercy. The correspondence is a hardened man who is opened. The escalation is that his conversion is a first instalment of a larger future, 11:15 and 11:26. The type falls short, because one man is a sign and not a guarantee, which is why Paul gathers further witnesses in the Scriptures.

typology.type: Israel's table turned into a snare
typology.fulfillment: In David's psalm the table that should have been a place of fellowship becomes a trap for those who oppose the righteous sufferer. The psalm pictures a suffering king who is mocked and given vinegar for his thirst, Psalm 69:21, and the Gospels apply that detail to Jesus, Matthew 27:34. The correspondence is that blessings misused become judgment. The escalation is at the table of the Lord, where Paul warns that eating and drinking in an unworthy manner brings judgment, 1 Corinthians 11:27-29. The type falls short in that the psalm's curse is a prayer against enemies, and Paul does not use it to wish harm on Israel but to describe the weight of refusal.

study.christ:
Paul does not mention Christ by name in the opening verses of Romans 11, but everything depends on Him, and the passage becomes clearer when the Gospel story stands behind it. The remnant is a remnant because of what happened to a single Israelite. In Isaiah 49:3 the LORD says to His Servant, 'You are My Servant, Israel,' and then the Servant's task is to bring Jacob back to God, Isaiah 49:5-6. The nation is reduced to one, who is Israel in person and who then gathers the rest. Matthew sees Jesus walking through Israel's own history, called out of Egypt, Matthew 2:15, tested in the wilderness for forty days, Matthew 4:1-2, and Paul says Christ was 'a servant of the circumcised' to confirm the promises to the patriarchs, Romans 15:8. The true remnant is the Faithful One, and the other members of the remnant are those united to Him.

Paul's phrase 'chosen by grace' also leads to Him. Ephesians 1:4 says believers were chosen 'in Him,' not apart from Him, so the election in verse 7 is election in the Son. Nothing in the passage allows a remnant that is saved outside Christ, and verse 7 is only the finish of what chapter 10 said: the stumbling stone is Christ and the righteousness that Israel could not find by works is found in Him, 9:30-33 and 10:4. What Israel was seeking, a righteous standing, is a person.

Christ is also the one who bears the hardening and the curse. The psalm Paul quotes in verses 9 and 10 is a psalm of a righteous sufferer whom the New Testament knows as Jesus: He is the zealous one whom the house of God consumed, John 2:17, the one hated without a cause, John 15:25, and the one whose reproach the Lord bore, Romans 15:3. In a way Paul does not himself draw out, the same Psalm that speaks of the trap for the unbelieving also speaks of the Messiah who goes under the weight, which makes the passage solemn: those who refuse are refusing the very sufferer who bears their sin.

Lastly, the risen Christ is the reason there is a remnant at all. Paul, who stands as living proof, was met by Jesus on the Damascus road and turned from persecutor to servant, Acts 9:3-6 and Galatians 1:15-16. The remnant is therefore the fruit of the resurrection, the first harvest of those whom the exalted Lord is gathering. In the same way the later promise of Romans 11:26, that the Deliverer will come from Zion, shows Christ at the end of the story as well as the centre. It guards against reading the remnant as a mere sociological fact. The remnant is a people who belong to the Messiah of Israel and who therefore carry Israel's hope forward.
study.god:
This passage shows a God who keeps a promise at cost to Himself and who takes no credit from the human side. The verse that matters most for the doctrine of God is verse 29's later statement, but its first form is here: 'God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew.' He is faithful to a people who have given Him ample reason to leave. That is not indulgence. It is the covenant love of Deuteronomy 7:7-8, which says the LORD set His affection on Israel not because it was large or strong but because He loved them and kept an oath.

The passage also shows a God who is more attentive than His servants. Elijah, a man of passion who had stood on Carmel, was wrong about the number of the faithful by a wide margin. God does not rebuke him sharply here; He corrects the record gently and then gives him work, 1 Kings 19:15-16. The quiet voice at Horeb is the context, 1 Kings 19:12, and Paul uses the story to teach that God sees what no prophet can.

Third, the passage forces the question of grace. A God who reserves a remnant 'for Himself' acts from His own initiative. Verse 6 states the principle as a matter of what grace is, and the implication is that God is free in the best sense: He is not bound by human merit and He is not hostage to human failure. This is the freedom of a Giver. It protects the dignity of grace and also the security of the saved, since what He started by choice He is not going to abandon because of their faults.

Fourth, the passage holds severity and mercy in one hand. The hardening of verse 7 is a real judgment, and Paul does not soften the quotations. A God who gave a 'spirit of stupor' is not a benign spectator. Yet the same sentence holds the phrase 'to this very day,' and the chapter that follows will show that His design is not to destroy. Divine judgment in Scripture is rarely a last word; it is often the road to a larger mercy, as with the exile, which ended in return.

For worship, the passage invites two responses. One is humble gratitude, since every believer is in the position of the seven thousand, kept by another's hand. The other is patience with the long ways of God. Elijah's story shows that discouragement is a real temptation of the faithful, and Paul's answer is not a pep talk but a revelation of what God was already doing in secret.

crossReferences.note: The scene at Horeb that Paul cites. Elijah says twice that he alone is left, and God replies by sending him back to work and telling him about the seven thousand. Note that the reply comes after the still small voice, so the lesson of the passage is that God's work often looks smaller and quieter than the prophet expects.

The promise that the LORD will not forsake His people nor abandon His heritage. Paul's question in verse 1 repeats its terms in the negative, and his 'Certainly not' answers with the psalm's own certainty. The psalm sits among those that call on God to judge the proud, so the trust in it is a trust that holds in dark times.

Samuel tells a frightened people that for the sake of His great name the LORD will not abandon them because He was pleased to make them His own. The ground is God's own name and pleasure, not Israel's performance, which is exactly Paul's ground for the remnant of grace.

The remnant that will rely on the LORD and return, with a warning that only a remnant will. Paul had already quoted verses 22 and 23 in Romans 9:27-28. Isaiah holds judgment and hope together, which is the double shape of Romans 11.

One of the two sources of Paul's composite quotation in verse 8, the 'spirit of deep sleep' that shuts the eyes of prophets and seers. Isaiah describes a people who read the vision as a sealed book. The hardening Paul describes is therefore not new but a repeat of what Isaiah saw in Jerusalem.

The other source of the composite quotation. Moses reminds Israel that they saw the signs in Egypt and yet 'to this day' had not been given a mind to understand, eyes to see or ears to hear. Paul reuses 'to this day' to make the point that the spiritual blindness in his time is the old condition, not a fresh invention.

David's prayer that the table of his persecutors become a snare and that their eyes be darkened. The Gospels read the psalm of Jesus again and again, so Paul's use brings the sufferer and the unbeliever together in the same chapter. It is solemn, and it must be read with Paul's own ache in Romans 9:1-3 beside it.

Paul's own account of his Hebrew credentials, including the tribe of Benjamin. Put beside Romans 11:1 it shows why he can say 'I am an Israelite myself' and mean it. What the later letter counts as loss for the sake of Christ, the earlier letter treats as evidence that God has not discarded His people.

Paul's earlier citation of Isaiah on the remnant. There the point was that only a remnant of the sand-like multitude would be saved and that the remnant keeps Israel from Sodom's fate. In Romans 11 the same remnant is moved from warning to evidence of hope.

The classic statement that salvation is by grace through faith, not from works, so that no one can boast. Verse 6 of Romans 11 states the same logic in a few words. The two texts share one grammar of grace, one with an eye on Gentiles and one on Israel.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is repeatedly one of collapse and preservation. After the flood a family is left, Genesis 7:23. After Egypt's famine a family is preserved by Joseph, Genesis 45:7. After the apostasy of the northern tribes a remnant remains, and after exile a remnant returns, Ezra 9:8. Each time the line of the promise passes through a narrow gate, and each time it widens again. The Elijah story in Romans 11:2-4 is one of the clearest illustrations, because it shows what the narrowing feels like from the inside: a prophet who is convinced the story is over.

Paul places his own time in that pattern. The Messiah has come, the gospel has gone out, and the majority of Israel has not believed. To someone who knew the earlier pattern, this would be unsurprising: there is a remnant, and the remnant is the seed from which a larger harvest will come. The story of Israel is thus continuous. The remnant of Paul's day is not a new people but the same one, and the church of Jewish and Gentile believers is a growth on the same root, as Paul will say in verses 16 to 24.

The passage also answers a question that Genesis raised. Why does God choose? In Genesis 12 God chooses Abraham for the sake of the nations. The remnant theme extends this: the few are chosen not as ends but as means, so that blessing can pass through. Paul's contention is that the few of his day are the first of the many. In the next verses he says that Israel's stumbling has opened the door to Gentiles, and that the Gentiles' faith is meant to provoke Israel to return.

Looking forward, the remnant ends in the multitude. The Bible's last chapters show a crowd no one can count, Revelation 7:9, and the remnant theme tells us how it began: a handful kept by grace, and then more. In the new creation the idea of a remnant dissolves into fullness, as in Romans 11:12, 'how much greater riches will their fullness bring.' The one who counts the faithful is the one who keeps them, and no member of the redeemed will have been there on the strength of their own record. Grace is the beginning, the middle and the end of the story, and that is why the passage can end with such heaviness over the rest and still be hope: it is set inside a plot whose last scene is mercy.

quiz.q: How does Paul answer the question, did God reject His people?

options.text: Certainly not; God has preserved a remnant, and Paul himself is proof.
options.note: Paul denies it emphatically and points to himself and to the remnant of grace.

options.text: Yes, God has finished with Israel and turned only to the Gentiles.
options.note: Paul flatly denies this; God has not rejected the people He foreknew.

options.text: Partly; God rejected the leaders but kept the ordinary people.
options.note: The division Paul draws is between the remnant of grace and the hardened, not leaders and people.

options.text: God has only postponed His rejection to a later day.
options.note: Paul speaks of present preservation, a remnant at the present time, not a delayed rejection.

quiz.q: What does the example of Elijah teach about the remnant?

options.text: Even when the faithful seem alone, God has kept a people for Himself by grace.
options.note: God had reserved seven thousand, just as He now keeps a remnant chosen by grace.

options.text: That faithful people are always a visible majority.
options.note: The remnant is the preserved few, not the impressive majority.

options.text: That God rescues only those who first prove their loyalty.
options.note: God reserved them for Himself; the emphasis is His keeping, not their prior proving.

options.text: That prophets are usually mistaken about their times.
options.note: Elijah misjudged how many were left, but the point is God's faithful preservation, not prophetic error.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say that if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works?

options.text: Because grace and works are opposite grounds; to mix them destroys grace.
options.note: Verse 6 states that if salvation were by works, grace would no longer be grace.

options.text: Because works come later, after grace has begun the process.
options.note: Paul is speaking of the ground of standing before God, which is grace alone, not a sequence.

options.text: Because good works have no place at all in the Christian life.
options.note: Works have their place as fruit; Paul's point is that they are not the basis of election.

options.text: Because grace is simply God rewarding our best efforts.
options.note: That would make grace a wage; Paul insists grace is free and unearned.

quiz.q: What happened to those in Israel who were not part of the remnant?

options.text: They were hardened, given eyes that could not see and ears that could not hear.
options.note: Verses 7 to 10 describe the hardening of the rest under God's righteous judgment.

options.text: They were immediately and finally destroyed.
options.note: Paul speaks of hardening, and later shows it is neither total nor final.

options.text: They were left completely neutral, neither helped nor hindered.
options.note: Scripture describes an active hardening, a spirit of stupor, not neutrality.

options.text: They were saved anyway apart from faith.
options.note: The hardened did not obtain what Israel sought; only the elect did.

quiz.q: On what basis is the remnant chosen?

options.text: By grace, God's free and unmerited favor, not by their works.
options.note: Paul says the remnant is chosen by grace, and grace excludes works.

options.text: By their superior obedience to the law.
options.note: If it were by works it would no longer be grace; obedience is not the basis.

options.text: By their descent from Abraham alone.
options.note: Physical descent is not enough; the remnant is chosen by grace, as Romans 9 has shown.

options.text: By a mixture of grace and personal merit.
options.note: Paul rules out any mixture; if it is by grace it is no longer by works.

questions: Paul points to himself as proof that God has not given up on His people. Where do you need to remember that God is faithful even when the situation looks hopeless?
Elijah thought he was the only faithful one left, but God had kept seven thousand. How does it encourage you to know that God is always preserving His people, even when you cannot see them?
The remnant is chosen by grace, not works. How would resting in God's free choice, rather than your own performance, change the way you relate to Him?
Verse 6 says grace and works cannot both be the ground of salvation. What are you tempted to add to grace as if it were not enough?
The hardening of the rest is a sobering judgment on unbelief. How does this move you to pray for those who cannot yet see, and to guard your own heart from becoming dull to God's word?

translationNotes.note: Whom He foreknew renders a verb that in Scripture means more than advance awareness; it carries the sense of God setting His covenant love on a people beforehand, an electing knowledge like that of Romans 8:29.

Some later manuscripts (BYZ and TR) add a second clause, But if it is by works, then it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work. The BSB follows the earlier text; the sense is unchanged, that grace and works are mutually exclusive as grounds of salvation.
The quotation blends Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10. A spirit of stupor renders a word for numbness or deep sleep; God gives the persistently unbelieving over to spiritual insensibility.
